grammar_notes.text: The vocalic phoneme inventory of Woccon can be reconstituted by examining Catawba cognates, indicating a similarity to Catawba but with the absence of certain Catawba phonemes. This suggests that these innovations occurred after the separation of Woccon and Catawba.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: By examining the Woccon words that have certain Catawba cognates, it is possible to reconstitute the phoneme inventory of Woccon. While this inventory is similar to that of Catawba, a number of Catawba phonemes are entirely lacking in Woccon.

grammar_notes.text: Woccon and Catawba show a difference in the distribution of long oral vowels and nasal vowels. In most cases, Woccon shows a long oral vowel where Catawba shows a nasal vowel.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: In most cases, it is Woccon that shows a long oral vowel where Catawba shows a nasal vowel. There are six such examples involving the vowels ã and ā; five cases involving the vowels i̓ and r̄, and two cases involving the vowels ũ and u̓.

grammar_notes.text: The consonantal phonemes of Woccon include p, t, k, (?), č, s, h, m, n, r̄, w, y. The phoneme b and d did not develop in Woccon as they did in Catawba.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Based on the available evidence, the consonantal phonemes of Woccon were p, t, k, (?), č, s, h, m, n, r̄, w, y; there is no evidence in Lawson’s vocabulary for assuming the phonemes b, d, š for Woccon.

grammar_notes.text: The phoneme ? is assumed to exist in Woccon but not attested due to limitations of English orthography used by early recorders.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: The phoneme ? is assumed for Woccon, although not attested in the data, since the phoneme is frequent in Catawba and English orthography did not provide early recorders with a good means for noting that consonant.

grammar_notes.text: Phonemes m and n do not change to b and d before oral vowels as they do in Catawba.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: As noted earlier, many instances of m and n became b and d, respectively, in Catawba before oral vowels, a change that did not occur in Woccon.

grammar_notes.text: There are cases where a Woccon word has a nasal vowel where the corresponding Catawba word has a long oral vowel. Examples include *á·haʔ? (W <Auhaun> ‘A Goose’: C á̓ha· ‘goose’), *ípa (W <Uu-coone> [error for <Un-poohe>] ‘Tobacco’; C ípa· ‘tobacco’).
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: There are also a few cases in which a Woccon word has a nasal vowel where the corresponding Catawba word has a long oral vowel. Examples include: *á·haʔ? ‘goose’ (W <Auhaun> ‘A Goose’: C á̓ha· ‘goose’), *ípa ‘tobacco’ (W <Uu-coone> [error for <Un-poohe>] ‘Tobacco’; C ípa· ‘tobacco’)

grammar_notes.text: Reduplication is used to signal frequency or intensity in Woccon, as seen with *sapí pé·ʔpe·ʔ? (‘mat’) and *yáp?lyap í:suwq (‘rundlet’). The reduplicated root forms are derived from the base roots |pe:?-| ‘step’ and ʔyap ‘tree’, respectively.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Examples include *sapí pé·ʔpe·ʔ? ‘mat’ (W ⟨Soppepepor⟩ ‘A Mat’: C sapí ‘on top’ plus pé·ʔpe·?, from the root |pe:?-| ‘step’ with frequentive reduplication) and *yáp?lyap í:suwq ‘rundlet’ (W ⟨Ynpyupseunne⟩ [error for ⟨Yupyupseunne⟩] ‘A Rundlet’: C ʔyap ‘tree’, with intensive reduplication, plus í:суwq ‘river’).

grammar_notes.text: In Woccon, the initial element ⟨Roo⟩ or ⟨Ru⟩ is used to form words referring to manufactured items. This element may be cognate with Catawba’s pronominal stem |ru-| and functions similarly to Catawba's prefix |dapa-|. Examples include *ruyú:ne·? (‘blanket’) and *rutípa (‘hoe’).
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Many of the words that refer to manufactured items in Lawson’s list begin with an element spelled ⟨Roo⟩ or ⟨Ru⟩. In most cases the part of the word that follows this initial element can be identified with a Catawba cognate lacking the initial element.

grammar_notes.text: Woccon words can be simple, composed of a single morpheme (e.g., *kus ‘corn’ [W ⟨Cose⟩ ‘Corn’: C kus ‘corn’], *wiʔtaʔ? ‘rat’ [W ⟨Wittau⟩ ‘A Rat’: C wiʔtaʔ? ‘rat’]) or complex, i.e., composed of two or more morphemes (e.g., *yéhu· ‘wind’ [W ⟨Yun-cor⟩ (error for ⟨Yuh-hor⟩)] ‘Wind’: C yéhu· ‘wind is blowing’ [from ye ‘air’ and hu· ‘come’]). As in Catawba, there is little phonological fusion of adjacent morphemes, and as a result, the morphemic composition of words is nearly always transparent.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: As in Catawba, Woccon words could be simple, i.e., composed of a single morpheme (e.g., *kus ‘corn’ [W ⟨Cose⟩ ‘Corn’: C kus ‘corn’], *wiʔtaʔ? ‘rat’ [W ⟨Wittau⟩ ‘A Rat’: C wiʔtaʔ? ‘rat’]) or complex, i.e., composed of two or more morphemes (e.g., *yéhu· ‘wind’ [W ⟨Yun-cor⟩ (error for ⟨Yuh-hor⟩)] ‘Wind’: C yéhu· ‘wind is blowing’ [from ye ‘air’ and hu· ‘come’]). As in Catawba, there is little phonological fusion of adjacent morphemes, and as a result, the morphemic composition of words is nearly always transparent.

grammar_notes.text: Both Woccon and Catawba also exhibit lexemes composed of two or more words, e.g., *íti tirú· ‘boulder’ (W ⟨Itte teraugh⟩ ‘Hard or heavy’, C ti tirú· ‘big stone, boulder’), *ruisap píswaʔ? ‘stockings’ (W [Rooesoo possoo] ‘Stockings’: C ísap ‘leggings, trousers’ plus pis ‘skin’ with the third person possessive suffix |–waʔ|). The order of terms in such compounds is head noun followed by modifier, the same pattern found in Catawba, suggesting that Woccon may have shared with Catawba the characteristics of an Object-Verb syntax.

The order of terms in such compounds is head noun followed by modifier, the same pattern found in Catawba, suggesting that Woccon may have shared with Catawba the characteristics of an Object-Verb syntax.

grammar_notes.text: The independent or indicative mode in Woccon is marked by the suffix |-re·|. This morpheme can be added to verbs, nouns, adverbs, adjectives, and particles to form a predicate. Examples include *kuwá:re· ‘he kills it’, *waʔčá:re· ‘there are nine’.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: The Catawba language possesses more than twelve suffixes to mark different modes (Siebert, 1941-52; Voorhis, 1984). Four of these modes appear to be attested in the Woccon data: the independent (or indicative), the participial, the imperative, and the interrogative.

grammar_notes.text: The participial mode in Woccon is marked by the suffix |-(a)?|. It can function both as an ending on verbs within a compound verbal construction and as a nominalizer. Examples include *íktaʔ? ‘bread’, *warápha? ‘one’s fever’.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Another frequent modal marker in Catawba is the participial, which has the form |-(a)?|. It is used both as an ending on one of the several verbs in a compound verbal construction and as a nominalizer. Woccon examples illustrating the participial mode are *íktaʔ? ‘bread’

grammar_notes.text: The imperative mode appears in two Woccon constructions. In *ni ku·ʔrá-te- (W: give me something to eat : C | ni ku-ʔ-ra-de-|), the voiced consonant of the Catawba imperative marker |-de-| results from intervocalic voicing, a process attested elsewhere in the Catawba language.

grammar_notes.text: The interrogative mode, which has the form |-ne| in Catawba, is attested in one Woccon word: *katé-ne (is that all?).

grammar_notes.text: In Woccon, the possessor of an alienably possessed noun is marked by a suffix. An example is *ruísap píswa? (stocking), where pis ‘skin’ has the third person possessive suffix |-waʔ|.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: While there are no clear examples of inalienably possessed nouns in the Woccon data, the three examples of alienably possessed nouns mark the possessor with a suffix. All of these examples involve the same word, marked for third person plural possession.

grammar_notes.text: The creation of voiced obstruent phonemes b and d from the denasalization of m and n, regressive assimilation of voicing in consonant clusters, and the subsequent introduction of onomatopoeic vocabulary containing the sounds b and d are late developments in Catawba. Woccon data confirm these changes were also late.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Internal reconstruction within Catawba and comparison of data from the two major dialects (Esaw and Saraw) suggest that the following changes were relatively late developments in Catawba: (1) the creation of voiced obstruent phonemes b and d from the denasalization of m and n, regressive assimilation of voicing in consonant clusters, and the subsequent introduction of onomatopoeic vocabulary containing the sounds b and d;

grammar_notes.text: The elimination of r from word-initial position through nasalization to n before nasal vowels and obstentiation to d before oral vowels is a late development in Catawba. Woccon data confirm these changes were also late.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: (2) the elimination of r from word-initial position through nasalization to n before nasal vowels and the obstentiation to d before oral vowels;

grammar_notes.text: The weakening of vowels in unstressed syllables, leading to syncope of unstressed short vowels is a late development in Catawba. Woccon data confirm these changes were also late.

grammar_notes.text: The Woccon word for 'Pease' is a contraction of the phrase kus sirá·k ‘corn-weed’. This pattern suggests that compound words in Catawba and presumably Woccon can be contracted into single forms.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: The Catawba word, and therefore presumably the Woccon word as well, is a contraction of the phrase kus sirá·k ‘corn-weed’.

grammar_notes.text: Woccon forms show intensive reduplication in words like 'Rundlet' (ʔyápʔyap í·suwa), indicating that a rundlet is a river heavily grown over with trees. This suggests the use of reduplication to emphasize or intensify meanings.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: The Woccon construction shows intensive reduplication of the word for tree indicating that a rundlet is a river heavily grown over with trees.

grammar_notes.text: In compounds, the initial syllable of the Catawba word 'grass' (sirák) is typically dropped. This pattern can be seen in words like 'Snake' (yáʔ?a·k), where only the first part of 'snake' and the second part of 'grass' are used.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: The initial syllable of the word for grass is typically dropped in compounds [cf. 1.36].

grammar_notes.source_excerpt: (The Woccon word contains the independent modal suffix, and thus literally means ‘there are nine’.)

grammar_notes.text: Presumably, Woccon has specialized the root as part of a digital counting system beginning with the little finger.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: (Presumably, Woccon has specialized the root as part of a digital counting system beginning with the little finger.)

grammar_notes.text: The Woccon form <Wonsh-shee> is derived from the Catawba root waq ‘arrow’ plus |-se| ‘end, point’. This suggests a morphological pattern where nouns can be formed by adding the suffix -se to denote an end or point.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Awl *wáse: W <Wonsh-shee> ‘Awl or Needle’; C waq ‘arrow’ plus |-se| ‘end, point’.

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root yá·če ‘ashes’ is cognate to the Woccon form <Yah-testea>, which means 'Black or Blue'. This indicates a possible phonological shift from č to t in Woccon.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Black *yá·če: W <Yah-testea> ‘Black or Blue, idem.’; C yá·če ‘ashes’. (Lawson used a wide variety of different grapheme combinations to render medial č for both Woccon and Tuscarora. The orthography in this word is one of the more unusual.)

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root nú·ne-? ‘blanket’ corresponds to the Woccon form <Roo-iune>, indicating a possible morphological pattern where nouns can be formed by adding -ne to denote a blanket.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Blankets *ruyú-ne-?: W <Roo-iune> ‘Blankets’; C nú·ne-? ‘blanket’

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root wátapi ‘bottle’ corresponds to the Woccon form <Wattape>, indicating a possible morphological pattern where nouns can be formed by adding -tapi to denote a bottle.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Bottle *wátapi: W <Wattape> ‘A Gourd or Bottle’; C wátapi ‘bottle’.

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root títi tirú- ‘big stone, boulder’ corresponds to the Woccon form <Itte teraugh>, indicating a possible morphological pattern where nouns can be formed by adding -tiru to denote a big stone or boulder.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Boulder *títi tirú-: W <Itte teraugh> ‘Hard or heavy’; C títi tirú- ‘big stone, boulder’.

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root iktáre- ‘they bake it’ corresponds to the Woccon form <Ikettau>, indicating a possible morphological pattern where nouns can be formed by adding -tau to denote bread.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Bread *iktá·?: W <Ikettau> ‘Bread’; C iktáre- ‘they bake it’. (The Woccon form is apparently a participle.)

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root yúhiya? ‘dress’ plus kíthaʔ ‘break in two’ corresponds to the Woccon form <Rooeyaukitte>, indicating a possible morphological pattern where nouns can be formed by combining dress and break in two.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Breeches *ruhiya-ʔ kíthaʔ: W <Rooeyaukitte> ‘Breeches’; C yúhiya? ‘dress’ (Saraw dialect) plus kíthaʔ ‘break in two’.

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root kú·wade- ‘come along!’ corresponds to the Woccon form <Quaute>, indicating a possible morphological pattern where verbs can be formed by adding -de to denote coming along.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Come along *kút-wate·: W <Quaake> (error for <Quaute>) ‘Will you go along with me?’; C kú·wade- ‘come along!’

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root kuwá·re- ‘he kills it’ corresponds to the Woccon form <Caure>, indicating a possible morphological pattern where adjectives can be formed by adding -ure to denote dead.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Dead *kuwá-re·: W <Caure> ‘Dead’; C kuwá·re- ‘he kills it’

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root tá·si ‘dog’ corresponds to the Woccon form <Taus-se>, indicating a possible morphological pattern where nouns can be formed by adding -se to denote dog.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Dog *tá·si: W <Tau-he> (error for <Taus-se>) ‘Dog’; C tá·si ‘dog’.

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root |-ra-| ‘eat’ corresponds to the Woccon form <Noccoo Eraute>, indicating a possible morphological pattern where verbs can be formed by adding -ra to denote eating.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Eat *|-ra-| . In W <Noccoo Eraute> ‘Have you got anything to eat?’; C |-ra-| ‘eat’. (See analysis in text.)

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root dábusa· ‘eight’ corresponds to the Woccon form <Nupsau>, indicating a possible morphological pattern where numbers can be formed by adding -sa to denote eight.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Eight *nápusa-: W <Nupsau> ‘Eight’; C dábusa· ‘eight’.

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root dapiné há·ksa-? ‘eleven’ corresponds to the Woccon form <Tonne hauk sea>, indicating a possible morphological pattern where numbers can be formed by adding -sea to denote eleven.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Eleven *tú há·ksaʔ: W <Tonne hauk pea> (error for <Tonne hauk sea>) ‘Eleven’, C dapiné há·ksa-? ‘eleven’.

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root wí·dyu- ‘meat’ corresponds to the Woccon form <Witso>, indicating a possible morphological pattern where nouns can be formed by adding -so to denote fawn-skin.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Fawn [meat] *wí·dyu·: W <Wisto> (error for <Witso>) ‘Fawn-skin’, C wí·dyu- ‘meat’.

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root yáču- ‘burnt firewood’ and yáhire- ‘he puts wood on the fire’ correspond to the Woccon form <Yau>, indicating a possible morphological pattern where nouns can be formed by adding -au to denote fire.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Fire *ya·: W <Yau> ‘Fire’; C yáču- ‘burnt firewood’, yáhire- ‘he puts wood on the fire’

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root yúhiyaʔ ‘dress’ (Saraw dialect) corresponds to the Woccon form <Rhiieyau>, indicating a possible morphological pattern where nouns can be formed by adding -yau to denote a flap.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Flap [Dress] *rúhiya·?: W <Rhiieyau> ‘A Flap’; C yúhiyaʔ ‘dress’ (Saraw dialect).

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root párapari ‘four’ corresponds to the Woccon form <Punnum-punne>, indicating a possible morphological pattern where numbers can be formed by adding -pune to denote four.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Four *párapari: W <Punnum-punne> ‘Four’; C párapari ‘four’.

grammar_notes.text: The Catawba root |-ku-| ‘give’ corresponds to the Woccon form <Noccoo Eraute>, indicating a possible morphological pattern where verbs can be formed by adding -ku to denote giving.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Give *|-ku-| : W <Noccoo Eraute> ‘Have you got anything to eat?’; C |-ku-| ‘give’. (See analysis in text.)

grammar_notes.text: The Woccon word for 'Sun or Moon' ends with the independent modal suffix |-re·|.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Either Woccon or Catawba has metathesized the first two syllables of this word. The Catawba word for star is a compound with | -nu- | 'egg, small roundish object'. The Woccon word ends with the independent modal suffix |-re·|.

grammar_notes.text: The ending on the Woccon form may be the interrogative mode marker, C | -ne | . If so, the gloss is 'That's all?'
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: (The ending on the Woccon form may be the interrogative mode marker, C | -ne | . If so, the gloss is 'That's all?')

grammar_notes.text: Woccon numeral forms can be combined with other numerals to create new numbers. For example, <Nommis-sau> (Seven) combines W <Nam-mee> (Three) plus an ending seen in Woccon (Nupsau) 'Eight'.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Seven *ná·msa-: W <Nommis-sau> 'Seven', W <Nam-mee> 'Three' plus the ending seen in Woccon (Nupsau) 'Eight'

grammar_notes.text: The Proto-Siouan initial *|wi-| is a pronominal element that marks non-human animates.

grammar_notes.text: The Woccon form appears to be the possessed form ‘your old woman’ with the second person singular prefix |yi-|.

grammar_notes.text: The third person singular affix |-h-| and the independent mode marker |-re·| are used to form *wičsuhire·, meaning 'he is (a) Windsor, he is English'.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: As suggested by Ralf Thiede, the Woccon word is perhaps derived from the surname Windsor, which later became the surname of the British royal family, with the addition of the third person singular affix |-h-| and the independent mode marker |-re·|

cultural_notes.text: Lawson was an explorer, not a linguist, and English orthography does not provide a distinctive means for writing nasal vowels, in particular before fricatives. Therefore, some cases of what appear to be long oral vowels in Lawson’s vocabulary may actually have been nasal vowels that either Lawson did not hear or that he did not bother to record.

cultural_notes.text: 'Rundlet' (Woccon: Yupyupseune) is described as a river heavily grown over with trees, indicating the importance of natural features in Woccon culture.
